To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the formation of the poor 3D-conductive phase LiTiO2 limits the theoretical maximum capacity of anatase Li(x)(TiO2) at room temperature to 0.6Li/TiO2.

the electronic and the ionic conductivity of LiTiO(2) are determined by the size of the particles and that this is due to the formation of a poor conducting LiTiO2 shell at the surface of larger particles, which limits the ionic diffusion and thus the capacity of the anatase LiTiO2 electrode.

(i) LiTiO2 is a good electronic conductor; (ii) LiTiO 2 is a poor ionic conductor; (iii) the maximum theoretical capacity is reached in LiTiO 4 crystallite sizes less then approximately 10 nm; and (iv) the maximum theoretical Li(x)Ti O2 capacity at room temperature is limited to approximately 0.5LiTiO2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental aspects of LiTiO(2) anatase, and the understanding of the limitations of the Li-ion insertion mechanism in TiO2 anataase.
the electronic and ionic structure of LiTiO 2, which is a key component in the development of new Li-ion battery materials.
the electronic and ionic properties of nanosized lithium intercalation compounds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the electronic structure of LiTiO 2, and the ionic diffusion of Li-ions in this compound, are the key factors which govern the performance of this compound as anode material for lithium batteries.

the electronic conductivity in nanoscale Li(x)Ti-oxide materials is not sufficient to allow for high rates (dis)charge of the Li-ion sites, and that the electronic conductivity is not the limiting factor in the ionic diffusion of lithium ions.
the LiTiO2 formation is not only limited to the nanoscale but also limited by its poor ionic conductivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the theoretical capacity for Li(x)Ti(1-x)O2 anatases is not reached in the bulk phase at room temperature and that the maximum capacity of Li(x)Ti1-xO2 can be obtained in crystallites of less than approximately 5 nm.

the Li-ion diffusion is too slow for the nano-sized materials to reach the theoretical capacity, and the Li-ion diffusion in the micro-sized materials is too slow to be able to reach the maximum theoretical capacity.

the electronic structure of Li(x)Ti(4+),Ti(3+),O2 is similar to the electronic structure of Ti(4+),O2, whereas the ionic conductivity of Li(x) Ti(4+),(3+),O(2) is significantly reduced compared to Ti(4+)(3+),O (2).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LiTiO2 formation is not only a function of the lithium content, but also of the crystallite size.
the electronic conductivity of the LiTiO2 is very high and that the ionic conductivity is very low.
nanoscale anatase Li(x)(TiO2) can be considered as a new type of Li-ion battery anode material.
